prize_parts.citation: for empirical evidence, built on transparent research designs, on how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, job polarisation and local labour markets

statement.case_for: I keep B009 as my single configuration, but I change the third name from Katz to Dorn. The criterion I stated at the outset is that the prize rewards a specific scientific contribution, not a career. The contribution is credible new evidence on a big question, paired with an account of what it means. The most precisely bounded version of B009 is the evidence on how trade exposure and technological change reshape labour demand and local labour markets. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the authors of that evidence. Autor and Dorn (2013) links task-based polarisation to local labour markets, so this trio also carries the technology strand through an empirical design and does not leave it out. The core designs have been re-run and challenged for more than a decade. The finding of large and persistent local adjustment costs has held, even where magnitudes are disputed. It changed how researchers and policymakers think about displacement and adjustment assistance. The citation can be worded to credit the evidence on labour demand and local adjustment, and to leave the task-based theory (Levy and Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo) uncredited by implication. On maturity and credit concentration, B009 is still clearly ahead of my former first choice, B050.
statement.case_against: The change costs something real. Katz anchors the long-run supply-and-demand evidence on the skill premium and wage structure (Katz-Murphy, Autor-Katz-Kearney). Dropping him narrows the prize toward one empirical programme and gives up part of the explanatory framework, which I value. The China-shock strand is also the part where persistence, magnitude, external validity and shift-share inference are still debated. Some members will see technology and trade as two achievements, and a trio drawn from one strand does not remove that charge. The task framework has co-originators who are not credited. The 2023 and 2024 prizes touch adjacent themes, and the citation has to be drafted narrowly to keep the discovery distinct from them. Dorn and Katz cannot both be credited under the three-name cap, and I am choosing between two defensible trios.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg moved from Autor-Hanson-Katz to Autor-Dorn-Hanson. She argues that Katz's education-and-technology work is closely tied to Goldin's research, recognised in 2023, and that Autor-Dorn (2013) already covers both the polarisation and trade strands.
responses.response: This argument moved me. I presented the 2023 prize, and its scope was the historical evolution of women's labour-market outcomes. The Goldin-Katz work on the race between education and technology sits close to that ground, and I had not given the overlap enough weight. I would still not say that Katz's wage-structure work is Goldin's work, because Katz-Murphy and Autor-Katz-Kearney are distinct. But a citation without Katz has less marginal-recognition risk than one with him, and Autor-Dorn (2013) gives a single paper that spans polarisation and local labour markets. I also accept your view of B050. It is a strong data contribution, but I would hold it for a later cycle.

responses.point: Teorell proposes Autor, Hanson and Dorn and centres the discovery on the China-shock evidence. He says he would accept the Katz version if the committee defined the achievement as the broader technology, tasks and trade picture.
responses.response: In response to the chair's question, I now prefer the Dorn trio. My Katz preference rested on a broad definition of the discovery. I still think that definition has merit, but a tightly bounded achievement is easier to credit exactly. I do not share your view that the China-shock strand is free of reservations. Persistence and shift-share inference are open, and the citation should claim only what has replicated: large, persistent local adjustment costs, with magnitudes disputed. Your treatment of the task framework as outside the credited discovery is right, and I would draft the citation to the same effect.

responses.point: Krusell keeps Katz because a citation spanning technology, trade and wage inequality needs the anchor of the long-run skill evidence. He argues that the narrow China-shock variant rests on a less settled evidentiary base and gives up the conceptual contribution, though he calls Autor-Dorn-Hanson a coherent variant.
responses.response: I take the conceptual loss seriously, and it is the main cost of my change. I would answer in two ways. First, the debate you describe has concerned size, persistence and inference. The existence of large local adjustment costs has survived it, and survival under that much scrutiny is itself evidence of maturity. Second, Autor-Dorn-style polarisation evidence keeps the technology mechanism inside the citation. I do not think either trio is clearly wrong. If the committee prefers the broader framing, Autor, Hanson and Katz remains a defensible choice, and I would not treat the difference as a matter of principle.

responses.point: Enflo keeps Katz because the citation should cover the framework as well as the shock. She says Dorn's claim on the China-shock papers is as strong as Hanson's, and that she would not oppose the Dorn trio if the trade-shock evidence is judged the primary discovery. She also warns against crediting Katz twice, given B050.
responses.response: I agree with your account of Dorn's role. My conclusion is that the primary discovery is the empirical evidence, and the interpretation can be drafted around it. On Katz in B050, I would not credit him in a second part. This configuration has one part, and B050 stays only an alternative, so the question does not arise. I also appreciate your maturity point on B050. It is part of the reason I prefer the older and much replicated body of work.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the discovery to be the empirical evidence on labour demand and local adjustment (Dorn) or the broader technology, tasks and wage-structure account (Katz). My choice is close and I hold it with moderate confidence.
How far the Goldin-Katz connection to the 2023 prize should reduce Katz's marginal claim, and how far the Acemoglu 2024 prize affects any task-related wording.
Persistence, magnitude and external validity of the China-shock estimates, and the inference properties of shift-share designs.
Whether the citation can credit the empirical evidence without implying credit for the task-based theory, which involves uncredited contributors.

Whether B014 would be the better-bounded achievement if the committee finds the B009 attribution too unsettled. Its main open issues are the uncredited priority claims of Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, and the welfare-gain critique.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz or the alternatives B014 and B050. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. My field proximity to labour economics and the economics of crime is not a documented personal connection to a candidate. For transparency, I presented the 2023 prize to Goldin at the announcement, and Katz is a long-time co-author of Goldin. I have no documented personal tie to Katz. Disclosed and not adjudicated, and no independent verification is claimed.
